#10455. Ukraine designed its own national typeface so it doesn’t have to use Russian fonts

Ukraine has had enough of Russian fonts.

Amid the country’s invasion by Russia, Ukrainians will no longer have to read any official documents set in a Russian typeface after a just-unveiled typeface goes into full effect. The new national font is called Zakon, “law” in Ukrainian.

Designers, military personnel, and Ukrainian citizens have for years called for their country to swap out Russian-designed Cyrillic fonts like Izhitsa, which appears on official documents, certificates, awards, diplomas, battle flags, and plaques, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture. Though the Russian font and others are widely used in Ukraine, they’re designed by the Russian type foundry ParaType, which Ukraine’s ministry says cooperates with Russian authorities.

To change that, Ukraine’s government and the country’s largest online jobs board partnered to hire a team of Ukrainian type designers to make something imbued with the country’s typographic heritage. A beta version of the font became available on October 29, and after a feedback period, a refined, expanded version is expected to be released early next year and will appear on official Ukrainian documents.

Ukraine’s parliament adopted a resolution in January to create the country’s own national typeface, saying that it would address the legacy of Russian cultural influence from when Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union.

A team of four Ukrainian type designers designed Zakon, which was unveiled last month in Cyrillic and Latin characters. The designers are Oleksiy Chekal, who designed lettering for the Orthodox Church of Ukraine; the typographic and type designer Hennadiy Zarechniuk; Dmytro Rastvortsev, who designed fonts including UAF Sans, for the Ukrainian military; and Andrij Shevchenko, a former winner of Ukraine’s modern business font competition.

Zakon is a serif typeface that features elements distinct to Ukrainian typography, like flared, asymmetrical serifs and diamond tittles that dot letters like I or Yi, a Cyrillic letter unique to Ukrainian. Its proportions resemble those of classical Roman typefaces, placing Ukrainian type within the wider European tradition. The type family’s letterform was inspired by the work of six Ukrainian artists, including Vasyl Krychevsky, who designed Ukraine’s 1918 trident coat of arms and banknotes.

These forms “help Ukrainians connect with their own visual heritage,” the Ukrainian Ministry of Culture tells Fast Company in a statement. “This matters because state awards, military battle flags, and government building signs in Ukraine are still often set in typefaces whose Cyrillic versions were produced by ParaType.”

The project was led by Taras Ishchyk, who previously designed the visual identity for the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Funding came from Ukraine’s largest online jobs board, Work.ua, which said it hoped its involvement shows that businesses can play an active role in shaping a country’s cultural landscape.

“A country’s visual language is more than its coat of arms and flag,” the company said in a statement. “The way letters appear in laws, orders, diplomas and awards also shapes the country’s image—and can either perpetuate someone else’s tradition or develop its own.”

Zakon has appeared in a promotional video for Ukraine’s national football (soccer) team, but its main purpose is for official documents and ceremonial papers. Full implementation will come after beta testing of how well it handles large volumes of text like official paperwork, newspaper layouts, and print publications.

Zakon text is free to download and use, and its makers are soliciting feedback about readability, weight, and performance at different sizes. Other versions of the font are exclusive, such as Zakon Decor for ceremonial inscriptions. Zakon Letterpress is reserved for use by Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada. Extended characters are expected to be released in early 2027, and the plan is to make it a multilingual typeface by releasing additional writing systems over the next year.

Ukraine blames centuries of policies from Moscow for erasing what made Ukrainian lettering distinct in the past, but Ukraine’s typographic style has been revived before, such as during its brief independence after 1917 as well as in the Ukrainian diaspora after World War II. Today, Zakon is reviving that tradition once again.

#10453. How Motion Design Improves SaaS Onboarding and Feature Adoption

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most SaaS products don't lose users because the software is bad. They lose users in the first few minutes, before anyone has seen what the product can actually do. Someone signs up, lands on an empty dashboard, feels a flicker of confusion, and quietly leaves. The industry has a name for the gap between signing up and getting value: activation. Closing it is one of the hardest problems in product design.

Motion design is one of the most underused tools for closing that gap. Used well, animation isn't decoration sprinkled on at the end. It's a layer of communication that tells users where to look, confirms that their actions worked, and makes a complex interface feel learnable instead of overwhelming. This article looks at why motion influences behaviour during onboarding, the specific patterns that move the needle on activation and feature adoption, and how to build them responsibly as a developer — with an eye on performance and accessibility throughout.

Motion works in onboarding because it speaks to how human perception actually operates, not because it looks modern. A few principles do most of the heavy lifting.

It directs attention. The eye is drawn to movement before it reads a single word. A gently pulsing button or an element that slides into view tells a new user where to go next without a paragraph of instructions. On a crowded first-run screen, that guidance is the difference between a confident first action and a confused exit.

It preserves context. When a panel expands, a card flips, or a new view slides in from the right, a short transition shows users where things came from and where they went. This spatial continuity keeps people oriented. Interfaces that snap instantly between states force the user to re-scan the screen each time and silently rebuild their mental model.

It confirms actions. Every click, toggle, and form submission is a small question: did that work? A quick visual response — a checkmark drawing itself, a row settling into place — answers it immediately. Without that feedback, users repeat actions, doubt the system, or assume something broke.

It shapes perceived performance. A thoughtful loading animation or skeleton screen makes a wait feel shorter and the product feel responsive, even when the underlying request takes exactly as long. Perception of speed is part of the experience, and motion is how you manage it.

These are the patterns that reliably help new users reach their first win.

Onboarding doesn't end after the first session. Most SaaS products keep shipping features, and each one faces its own adoption problem: users settle into a few familiar workflows and never discover the rest. Motion is how you reintroduce the product to people who already think they know it.

Contextual nudges that appear in motion — a tooltip that eases in near a newly relevant button, a gentle highlight on a feature the moment a user hits the limit it solves — are far more effective than a generic email. They arrive at the point of need and use movement to pull attention without hijacking the screen.

"What's new" reveals can announce an update with a small, well-timed animation rather than a modal that gets dismissed on reflex. A badge that animates in, or a panel that slides open on the first visit to a page, respects the user's flow while still being noticed.

Animated demonstrations carry the most weight for genuinely complex features. Showing a feature in motion — rather than describing it in text — lets users grasp a multi-step workflow in seconds. For intricate capabilities, this is where a short, purpose-made explainer earns its place, a point we return to in the next section.

The right tool depends on how complex the animation is and where it lives. Roughly in order of weight:

CSS transitions and keyframe animations should be your default. They cover the large majority of onboarding motion — hovers, state changes, highlights, progress bars — and the browser can run them efficiently. Reach for JavaScript only when CSS genuinely can't express what you need.

The Web Animations API gives you CSS-level performance with programmatic control, which matters when animations depend on data or user input, or need to be sequenced and interrupted. SitePoint's guide to the Web Animations API is a solid introduction, and the broader web animation archive covers libraries like GSAP for orchestrating complex timelines.

Lottie is the bridge between designer-made animation and the web. Designers export vector animations as JSON, and a lightweight player renders them natively at small file sizes — ideal for polished illustrative moments like success states and animated empty states, without hand-coding every frame.

Pre-rendered video is the right call when a feature is genuinely involved and a looping CSS animation or a tooltip simply can't carry the explanation. A short, well-produced walkthrough can compress a multi-step workflow into something a user absorbs in under a minute, which is why many teams lean on a dedicated SaaS explainer video for their most complex features and onboarding moments. The trade-off is weight and production effort, so reserve video for the handful of places where it genuinely outperforms in-interface motion, lazy-load it, and never autoplay it with sound.

Motion that stutters does more damage than no motion at all, and motion that ignores accessibility can actively harm users. Two disciplines keep animation on the right side of that line.

For performance, animate the properties the browser can handle cheaply: transform and opacity. These can run on the compositor thread without triggering layout or paint, which is what lets animation hold a smooth 60fps. Animating properties like width, height, top, or left forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame and is the usual cause of janky motion. Keep animations short — most interface transitions should land between 150 and 300 milliseconds — because motion that overstays its welcome makes a product feel slow.

For accessibility, honour the prefers-reduced-motion media query. Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or disorientation from movement, and the operating system lets them ask for less of it. Respecting that setting is straightforward:

Beyond that, never let an animation block interaction. If a user has to wait for a flourish to finish before they can click, the motion is working against them. Animation should support the task and then get out of the way.

Motion design is a product decision, so treat it like one and measure it. The metrics that matter map directly to the problems motion is meant to solve.

Treat animations as hypotheses and A/B test them. Ship the animated onboarding step to half of your new users and measure activation against the control. Motion should earn its place with data, not assumptions — and occasionally the data will tell you an animation is slowing people down, which is just as useful to know.

The best onboarding motion is the kind users never consciously notice. It simply makes the product feel clear, responsive, and easy to learn — guiding attention, confirming actions, and turning a complex interface into something approachable. That's the real payoff: not animation for its own sake, but fewer confused users, faster time to value, and features that actually get discovered.

Start small. Pick the single point in your onboarding where users most often stall, add one purposeful animation that removes the confusion, and measure what happens. Motion, used deliberately, is one of the most direct levers you have on activation and adoption — and like any good tool, it works best when it draws no attention to itself.

#10452. 5 things Jensen Huang mastered that Nvidia’s next CEO will have to learn

The tech world loves superhuman leaders who can withstand boardroom coups and weather negative publicity. Steve Jobs navigated negative press during his tenure at Apple. Elon Musk’s transgressions are forgiven by his followers because of what he brings to his companies. And Sam Altman survived a boardroom coup a little under three years ago.

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s one-of-a-kind CEO and figurehead since its founding in 1993, couldn’t survive reports of successive romance scandals. On November 12, he was defenestrated and replaced by his chief financial officer as interim CEO. But in the long term, a permanent replacement will be needed.

Finding the right person will be tricky. Huang was renowned for his attention to detail, larger-than-life leadership style, and outgoing personality. He deftly navigated competing business and geopolitical interests to build one of the world’s most valuable companies—and managed to master a wide range of disciplines along the way.

So what qualities will his successor have to replicate?

Managing geopolitics

Huang’s downfall began with a dalliance with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, the CEO of tech company Megaspeed. But one of his biggest strengths was his ability to navigate the messy geopolitics of the AI race between the U.S. and China—and the awkward relationship between Taiwan, home to TSMC, which is central to Nvidia’s chipmaking process, and China, which wants to invade it.

“The fact that he was born in Taiwan, is the founder-CEO of Nvidia, and has been able to advocate for less-hawkish approaches to tech policy vis-a-vis China all go hand in hand in giving him perspectives as well as influence within the White House, and a demigod status in Taiwan and Asia,” says Kristy Loke, a researcher at the MATS Program. Loke reckons any future CEO will struggle to replicate that geopolitical deftness. “Instead of Steve Jobs, we’ll get perhaps a Tim Cook,” she says.

Handling Donald Trump

Game recognizes game, and Donald Trump held Jensen Huang in high esteem. The U.S. president was still defending Huang earlier this week, saying his departure wasn’t necessary.

“Between Taiwan and the development of AI in the U.S. and China, Huang has attempted to walk a careful line between the Chinese and U.S. governments, refusing to use adversarial language with respect to China, and uniquely able to attempt to remind political leaders of the major dependence of Nvidia on Asian supply chains and markets,” says Paul Triolo, partner and head of technology for Asia and the Americas at DGA.

That could easily have irked the man in the White House. But it didn’t. “He was clearly a staunch supporter of the U.S. leading in the AI race, and frequently only advocated for the sale of GPUs to China several generations behind the cutting edge to ensure the U.S. lead,” says Triolo. “These are policies that both the Biden and Trump administration have supported.”

Being a personality and pitchman

Nvidia didn’t become one of the world’s most valuable companies by accident, and one of Huang’s strengths was his ability to convince a skeptical public that AI was a technology worth investing in. Like Steve Jobs with his iconic black turtleneck, Huang had his own trademark look—along with the swagger to match—that helped make him one of AI’s most recognizable personalities.

One suggestion for his replacement has come from the White House, where Donald Trump has floated Apple’s former CEO, Tim Cook, as a potential candidate to lead Nvidia. That seems unlikely.

Schmoozing clients and customers

Huang’s downfall stemmed from getting too close to his contacts, but one of his strengths as CEO was his ability to keep people sweet. Taiwanese media regularly covered Huang’s wining and dining of clients, which sometimes involved trips to street food stalls and getting chummy with collaborators.

The concept is known as 义气, which roughly translates to loyalty. Huang made regular visits to his native Taiwan, home to many of the vendors that supply Nvidia with chip components, maintaining those relationships through boozy meals and appearances at factory ribbon-cutting ceremonies. That closeness paid dividends. “Jensen’s legendary supply chain dinners and commitments are what pushed suppliers in Taiwan to deliver on technologically and logistically aggressive plans,” wrote Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis in a blog post. It’s much less clear whether those suppliers will extend the same warmth to anyone else.

Keeping on top of the details

Beyond his command of the big picture, one thing that distinguished Huang from many CEOs was his deep understanding of how his business worked and the technology underpinning it. “He was much more involved in the details of the firm’s day-to-day operations than a typical CEO and has no deputies who can easily step into his shoes,” says Chris Miller, a researcher at Tufts University and the author of Chip War, a book on the semiconductor industry.

That strength may now prove a weakness, as Huang’s flat organizational structure means few others possess the same combination of breadth and depth of expertise. “Jensen Huang was one of the longest serving CEOs in the tech industry and the key force behind Nvidia’s rise and its investments in AI,” says Miller. “He’ll be very hard to replace.”

#10449. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

#10448. Microsoft’s massive outage puts its AI-driven layoffs under scrutiny

Microsoft’s massive service outage on Thursday left businesses and government agencies scrambling to access critical services. It also came at an awkward moment for the tech giant, which has undertaken an extensive initiative to reduce its workforce even as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence.

Recent efforts to trim the company’s head count included extending buyout offers to 9,000 U.S. employees in April and 60,000 employees in four countries in October. It also laid off 4,800 workers in July, mostly in its sales and Xbox divisions. Last month, The Information also reported that leadership in Microsoft’s Azure cloud division had discussed cutting costs by at least 20%; Microsoft denied the report.

Meanwhile, the company is pouring billions into AI infrastructure. Earlier this year, it projected roughly $190 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, much of it driven by the enormous computing demands of AI and cloud services.

Fast Company has reached out to Microsoft for comment.

There is no evidence that either the workforce reductions or AI investments directly contributed to Thursday’s disruption. But the incident raises a broader question for Microsoft and the tech industry: As businesses shrink their workforces and increasingly rely on AI to boost productivity, are they also risking the reliability of their existing products? 

Workforce reductions and restructurings can push out experienced employees who understand how a company’s systems work, including any longtime bugs or quirks, and who know how to respond when something breaks. Even if layoffs don’t directly cause technical problems, the loss of institutional knowledge can make those problems harder to solve.

Enacting such reductions while also adapting to a rapidly changing technology like AI may be especially risky. As companies reorganize around these new tools, fewer resources may be available to maintain and troubleshoot existing systems. 

The challenge is particularly acute for massive tech companies such as Microsoft, whose sprawling infrastructure includes decades-old systems alongside cutting-edge AI services.

Microsoft and many other firms are also betting that AI allows smaller teams to maintain or increase their productivity. But that doesn’t necessarily translate into greater reliability. Keeping complex systems running requires experienced employees who can anticipate failures and understand how different components interact, especially when something goes wrong.

And for technology companies, the burden falls not only on humans but on the machines themselves. As companies expand AI services and add new layers of infrastructure, their systems become more complex, and potentially more vulnerable, which could make outages more difficult to prevent or contain.

While the root cause of this week’s disruptions remains to be seen, the incident is a reminder of the stakes at hand in Microsoft’s transformation. To succeed, it not only has to accomplish more with fewer workers, but must also do so without sacrificing the services its customers already depend on.

#10446. Android XR glasses officially get a December release date [Video]

Following a pre-order date announcement earlier this week, Google’s other Android XR launch partner has now confirmed a December release date for this first batch of glasses.

Earlier this week, Warby Parker revealed that its first Android XR glasses will go up for pre-order next week on November 12, also reiterating the “Intelligent Eyewear” branding that Google and Samsung are using for these devices.

Following up on that, the other design partner has confirmed a release date for its first Android XR glasses.

Gentle Monster posted a teaser on Twitter/X for a short film starring Joaquin Phoenix that is “a cinematic journey between reality and dream.” The full film will be released in “mid-November,” almost surely on that November 12 date, but that’s not the interesting part here – and that’s saying something, because interesting is more definitely a fitting description of the video.

Gentle Monster’s first Intelligent Eyewear collection⠀Joaquin Phoenix stars in a short film directed by Jonathan Glazer—a cinematic journey between reality and dream. Full film releasing mid-November.⠀The collection launches this December.⠀Register for the collection… pic.twitter.com/UBv6pdHWSW

Rather, it’s the casual mention of the release date for Gentle Monster’s Android XR glasses. Well, release window. It’s been rumored, but this is the official confirmation that the first Android XR glasses are getting a December 2026 release date. Better late than never, though it’s certainly interesting to see a product launch so late in the year.

Warby Parker hasn’t mentioned a December release date yet, but it stands to reason we’ll see the same launch window.
